Rephaiah
reh-FYE-uh
proper noun
Hebrew Rephayah (H7509), the LORD heals — from rapha (H7495), to heal, to cure, to restore, and Yah, the covenant name; the same verb in I am the LORD that healeth thee (Exo 15:26).

Biblical Definition

Five men bear this name. One stands in the royal line of Judah after the captivity (1Ch 3:21); one is a captain of the Simeonites who went up to mount Seir (1Ch 4:42); one is a son of Tola of Issachar, head of a father's house among men reckoned valiant men of might in their generations (1Ch 7:2); one is a Benjamite in Saul's genealogy (1Ch 9:43); and one is Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, who took his place on the wall under Nehemiah (Neh 3:9). That last is the most striking. A man with civil authority over half the capital picked up a trowel and repaired his section like everyone else. Nehemiah's register names rulers, priests, goldsmiths, apothecaries, merchants and daughters, all on the same wall. The name means the LORD heals, and healing in Scripture is never merely physical: Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed (Jer 17:14); he healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds (Psa 147:3); and of the Servant, with his stripes we are healed (Isa 53:5).

Origin & Era

The name of five men, including the ruler of half of Jerusalem who repaired a section of the wall under Nehemiah. It means the LORD heals.

expand to see more

REPHAIAH, Hebrew Rephayah, the LORD heals.

1. A descendant of David in the royal line after the captivity.

2. A captain of the Simeonites who smote the Amalekites in mount Seir.

3. A son of Tola of the tribe of Issachar, head of a father's house.

4. A Benjamite in the genealogy of Saul. 5. Son of Hur, ruler of the half part of Jerusalem, who repaired the wall.

Key Scripture

Neh 3:9 — "And next unto them repaired Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem."

1Ch 7:2 — "And the sons of Tola; Uzzi, and Rephaiah, and Jeriel, and Jahmai, and Jibsam, and Shemuel, heads of their father's house, to wit, of Tola: they were valiant men of might in their generations; whose number was in the days of David two and twenty thousand and six hundred."

1Ch 3:21 — "And the sons of Hananiah; Pelatiah, and Jesaiah: the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shechaniah."

1Ch 9:43 — "And Moza begat Binea; and Rephaiah his son, Eleasah his son, Azel his son."

Modern Corruption

Healing is claimed as a right the believer may demand; Scripture makes it a mercy God gives, often deferred to the resurrection.

expand to see more

A large strand of modern teaching holds that physical healing is guaranteed in the atonement and available on demand to anyone with sufficient faith, so that continued sickness proves a defect in the sufferer. The pastoral cruelty of this is matched only by its distance from the text. Paul left Trophimus at Miletum sick (2Ti 4:20); Timothy was told to take a little wine for his stomach's sake and his often infirmities (1Ti 5:23); Epaphroditus was sick nigh unto death, and Paul ascribes his recovery to God's mercy rather than to anyone's technique (Php 2:27); and Paul's own thorn was not removed, with the answer given instead: My grace is sufficient for thee (2Co 12:9).

What Scripture does promise is that the LORD is the healer — I am the LORD that healeth thee (Exo 15:26) — that He is to be asked, and that the deepest healing is already accomplished: with his stripes we are healed, which Peter applies to the soul returning to the Shepherd (1Pe 2:24-25). The rest waits for the body's redemption, when there shall be no more pain (Rev 21:4). The principle to recover is that healing is a gift and not a lever, that every believer who has ever lived has eventually died, and that the God who has healed the worst of it may be trusted with the timing of the remainder.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Rephayah (H7509), from rapha (H7495), to heal, to restore, with Yah.

expand to see more

Hebrew rapha (H7495) — to heal, to cure, to make whole; I am the LORD that healeth thee (Exo 15:26).

Hebrew Rephayah (H7509) — borne by five men; 1 Chronicles 3:21, 4:42, 7:2, 9:43, Nehemiah 3:9.

Hebrew marpe (H4832) — a cure, health, a remedy; a sound heart is the life of the flesh (Pro 14:30).

Hebrew chabash (H2280) — to bind up; he healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds (Psa 147:3).

Greek iaomai (G2390) — to heal, to cure; by whose stripes ye were healed (1Pe 2:24).

Usage

"“Rephaiah the son of Hur, the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem”."

"“They were valiant men of might in their generations”."

"“Heal me, O LORD, and I shall be healed” (Jer 17:14)."
